Research in the Machine Learning and Autonomy for Diverse Domains (MADD) Lab on
detecting wildfires from autonomous UAVs, presented as a poster.

Existing wildfire monitoring leans on satellite thermal imagery, ground sensors,
and observation towers. These produce good data for understanding how a fire
*behaved*, but they tend to confirm fires rather than catch them — detection
often arrives after ignition. The proposal here is a low-cost drone carrying
both thermal and visual sensors, running detection onboard, so the latency
between "something is burning" and "someone knows" collapses.

## Platform

| Component | Role | Cost |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Holybro drone, Pixhawk 6C flight controller, GPS, telemetry radio | Airframe and flight control | ~$735 |
| NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (1024 CUDA cores) | Onboard inference | ~$250 |
| Intel RealSense depth camera (RGB + IR, 1280×800 @ 30 fps) | Visual detection | ~$314 |
| FLIR Lepton 3.5 (−10 °C to 110 °C) | Thermal imaging | ~$199 |

Keeping the whole sensor package under roughly $1,500 is the point, not a
footnote — the end goal is a *swarm*, and a swarm only makes sense if one node
is cheap enough to lose.

## Results So Far

The thermal and RGB computer-vision pipelines run a **YOLOv8** model, reaching
**up to 70% fire-detection accuracy**. Flight testing produced detections from
both modalities. On a frame from the
RealSense camera, a pre-trained object detector returned **twenty correct
detections against five misses**. Thermal capture from **300 feet above Foothill
Blvd** cleanly separated the warm road surface from the cooler trees around it,
which is the contrast a fire-detection model needs to key on.

## Contributions

- Designed an in-house drone system with low-cost thermal and visual sensors.
- Extended single-drone perception toward a swarm architecture.
- Deployed deep-learning fire-detection models on the Jetson Orin Nano for
  online inference.

Continued work scales to two or more drones, with the additional aircraft
carrying a Raspberry Pi and a different sensor mix to broaden the data collected
from a single fire.
